articles.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
articles.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances By Nikhil Inamdar Mumbai 
- Published 5 October 2026 
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China. 
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%. 
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked. 
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market. 
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world. 
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year. 
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC. 
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period. 
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI). 
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed 
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues". 
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC. 
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods. 
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones. 
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava. 
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment. 
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank. 
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production. 
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends. 
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output. 
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year. 
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components 
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies. 
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li. 
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same." 
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava. 
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short. 
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds. 
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India." 
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising. 
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds. 
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

articles.title: UK university asks staff to review some partnerships with China after MI5 warning
articles.summary: The UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Staff at QUB have been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI" By Robbie Meredith 
Education and arts correspondent, BBC News NI 
- Published 4 October 2026 
Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) has asked staff to review some partnerships with China after a warning from MI5. 
In a highly unusual move, the UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage. 
MI5 said the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) was a front company working for China's intelligence and security service. 
However, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated". 
Staff at Queen's have now been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI". 
"Work is ongoing within Queen's to do this," an email to staff said. 
"However, this may not be obvious through our existing systems and so researchers are also advised to undertake appropriate due diligence to identify the ultimate source of funding for collaborations with Chinese institutions." 
MI5 issued the alert for UK universities about CGTRI which it said had "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). 
Universities in the UK often collaborate and partner with universities elsewhere in the world to share research and expertise. 
But MI5 said it had identified more than 100 UK-linked academics who had contributed to projects funded by Ministry of State Security via CGTRI. 
It said that in some cases the researchers would not be aware of the front company's role in their project. 
UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. 
MI5 added that academics who failed to cut ties with CGTRI could ultimately face criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. 
As a result, UK universities were advised to immediately review the funding of any research collaboration with China. 
A QUB spokesperson told BBC News NI that the university takes "responsibilities around research and national security extremely seriously". 
"Queen's University has commenced a review around any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI," they said. 
"We have also contacted staff requesting they review any existing or proposed collaborations with them and report any concerns to the relevant Faculty Dean of Research. 
"We will keep this situation under review while continuing to support our collaboration, research and innovation projects locally, nationally and internationally." 
According to its website, QUB has invested over $10m (£7.56m) in China-related research in areas like sustainable energy, information technology, food security and cancer research over the past decade. 
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Ulster University said they had no research links with the organisation referenced by MI5.

articles.title: Indian singer Anuv Jain on finding success without the Bollywood boost
articles.summary: The star reveals why he is "very selective" about releasing music - and shares his future collab hopes.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Meghan Katti Image caption, 
The singer-songwriter has opened up about building a career on India's music scene as an acoustic indie pop performer By Srosh Khan   and   Naomi de Souza ,  BBC Newsbeat 
- Published 5 October 2026 
Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you? 
Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful". 
The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene. 
BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best". 
"It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse. 
But they do tell a story. 
Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager. 
His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak. 
Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing. 
Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives , external and is personal to them. 
His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify. 
According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple. 
When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song. 
"I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says. 
"For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this." 
Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists. 
He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry. 
Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space". 
"We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says. 
Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success. 
Image source, Meghan Katti Image caption, 
At one point, Jain was only releasing one song a year 
Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently. 
But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon". 
"They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says. 
"It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out." 
The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out. 
"There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet. 
"When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it." 
Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages , external of Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram. 
Image source, Meghan Katti Image caption, 
The singer also plays the guitar and has become known for his songs about deep emotions and themes 
There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years. 
Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way". 
"The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says. 
But, he adds: "I'm not there yet". 
However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart. 
"He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain. 
"Maybe the universe will just make it happen."

articles.title: FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader’s family for China
articles.summary: Wanying Zhang surveilled Taiwanese president’s son and family for China while in US, according to FBIThe FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles international airport (LAX) as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president’s family for China.Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
FBI agents with Wanying Zhang on 4 October, as seen in a screengrab from a video released on US attorney Bill Essayli’s X account. Photograph: X account of US Attorney Bill Essayli/AFP/Getty Images 
View image in fullscreen 
FBI agents with Wanying Zhang on 4 October, as seen in a screengrab from a video released on US attorney Bill Essayli’s X account. Photograph: X account of US Attorney Bill Essayli/AFP/Getty Images 
FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader’s family for China
Wanying Zhang surveilled Taiwanese president’s son and family for China while in US, according to FBI 
The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles international airport (LAX) as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president’s family for China . 
Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI. 
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China without registering as a foreign agent as legally required, first assistant US state attorney Bill Essayli of California’s central federal district announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said. 
Citing real-estate licensing and listing records, the Los Angeles news outlet KTLA reported that Zhang was a licensed real-estate salesperson based in the southern California city of Irvine. 
She was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China . Her nationality was not clear, and it was also not immediately clear if she had an attorney representing her. 
She was due to appear on Monday in federal court in Los Angeles . 
Taiwan’s presidential office confirmed relatives of the Taiwanese president, Lai Ching-te were the targets. The office did not specify if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression”. 
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts – which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families – as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement. 
The Chinese embassy in the US did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. And the foreign ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays. 
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949. But China claims the island as part of its own territory. 
Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and China do not belong to each other. He also has said the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan”. 
China considers Lai a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace”. 
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan – notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system. 
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title: UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
articles.summary: Move would strengthen Britain’s case to be included in new legislation to protect European manufacturingBusiness live – latest updatesThe UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals.It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Chinese cars such as the Jaecoo 7, built by Chery, are selling well in the UK. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
Chinese cars such as the Jaecoo 7, built by Chery, are selling well in the UK. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters 
UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
Move would strengthen Britain’s case to be included in new legislation to protect European manufacturing 
- 
Business live – latest updates 
The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals. 
It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation , known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. 
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely . Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024. UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets 
Read more 
Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU. 
It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024. 
The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector. 
A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”. 
If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing. 
The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain. 
China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations. 
Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off” , with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers. 
However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain. 
Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties. 
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences. 
“The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.” 
Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures. 
BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday. 
In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000. 
Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far. 
A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”
